growth_story.headline: Burkina Faso's income per person has grown about 2.4 percent a year since 1990, through the move from cotton to gold, spreading insecurity and military coups.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, income per person in Burkina Faso has grown at a steady 2.4 percent a year with no lasting shift up or down, and in 2025 it reached its highest level yet. The pace was 2.4 percent in 2006–2015 and 2.3 percent in 2016–2025. The big swings came in single years: 8.2 percent in 1996, close to zero in 2009, and falls of -0.4 percent in 2020 and -0.7 percent in 2022. World Bank work describes fast growth in total output over the past two decades, as the economy moved from cotton exports to gold, but the population grew so quickly that income per person rose much more slowly. Insecurity linked to the Malian crisis that began in 2012 disrupted farming and gold mining, and two military coups followed in 2022; growth in income per person was only 0.7 percent in 2023. A strong harvest and high gold prices brought a recovery, with income per person up 2.5 percent in 2024 and 3.0 percent in 2025.

threads.title: From cotton to gold
threads.text: Over the past two decades the economy moved from relying on cotton exports to relying on gold, which left it exposed to global shocks. Industrial gold mining became a driver of growth, but it creates few jobs and has few links to local businesses. The World Bank dates the end of Burkina Faso's catch-up with regional peers to around 2013.

threads.title: Insecurity and military rule
threads.text: Insecurity spread across Burkina Faso and two military coups followed in 2022; the uncertainty and violence shut the zinc mine for good and closed several gold mines for a time. Attacks have become less frequent, but many people remain displaced or short of food, and insecurity still disrupts markets and private investment.

threads.title: The gold price windfall
threads.text: High world gold prices lifted economic activity in 2025, and gold dominates exports and is an important source of public revenue, though it creates few jobs. A new mining code changed the state's stake, permit terms and local content rules, and the IMF reports that it held back the rebound in mining output that year.

threads.text: Most people work in farming that depends on rain and has low productivity, which leaves rural livelihoods exposed to swings in the weather. The population has grown quickly, so fast growth in total output has turned into much smaller gains in income per person.

since_last_year.text: High gold prices lifted growth in 2025, and income per person rose 3.0 percent to its highest level yet. In 2026 the picture became less certain. The World Bank expects slower farm growth after late rains and costlier fertilizer, and the IMF describes a shock from fertilizer and energy prices, spillovers from the armed groups' offensive in Mali and a drop in humanitarian aid.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes total output growing fast for two decades, a pace very few low-income countries matched, yet income per person has risen only about 2.4 percent a year since 1990 because the population grew so quickly. The sources also describe a deepening security crisis and two military coups, but the data show no lasting break: the last decade averaged 2.3 percent against 2.4 percent in the decade before, and the damage shows up only in single weak years such as -0.7 percent in 2022 and 0.7 percent in 2023.
